newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Troubled Hungarian banks up for sale.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Troubled Hungarian banks up for sale.

text.p: Hungary is about to sell two of its biggest banks and says buyer interest is keen, even though one of them made the largest loss in Hungarian history.

"Somehow the climate has changed," said Istvan Abel, managing director for financial institutions at APV Rt, the privatisation agency, which hopes this autumn to sell off Magyar Hitel Bank Rt (MHB) and Kereskedelmi es Hitelbank (K&H).
Abel was referring to the dark days in 1995 when the government waited anxiously while Credit Suisse pored over the books at Budapest Bank for six months, only to pull out.

Since then, Hungary has sold a 60 percent stake in Budapest Bank to GE Capital and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). APV also reduced its stake to 25 percent plus one vote in OTP, Hungary's biggest commercial bank.

Now it hopes to sell K&H and MHB, even though MHB officials say the bank made $1.5 billion in losses from 1992 through 1994. The APV announced on Thursday it would offer an 89 percent state MHB to strategic investors in September.

The sales have generated considerable interest, particularly in MHB. ABN Amro Bank NV of the Netherlands, Austria's Creditanstalt-Bankverein, Bank Austria and Citibank are among potential buyers cited by analysts and bank sources.
Abel credits a change in government policy with the increase in buyer interest since the Budapest Bank fiasco.
"No one knows (why Credit Suisse) withdrew but country risk was I think the worst factor," Abel told Reuters.

"Policy then recognised it's impossible to insist on certain issues like strategic buyers. We need to accept financial investors or whoever is willing to buy. Privatisation is so vital that we can't be so choosy any longer."
It may seem an odd time to buy a Hungarian bank, when the market share for Hungarian-owned banks has slipped from 100 percent in the communist era to under 30 percent today.
There are now some 40 foreign-owned banks operating in Hungary which have gobbled up the bulk of corporate clients.

But Zsigmond Jarai, who took over as MHB's chief executive officer in 1995, says institutions like his have a lot to offer, particularly since MHB reported an after-tax profit of 2.7 billion forints ($18 million) for the first half of 1996.
"No one in Hungary believed that we were going to make that," Jarai said, adding that the bank is aiming for $30 million profit for the year.

Jarai said MHB has cleaned house -- writing off millions of dollars of bad debt, cutting staff by 40 percent to 2,500 and reducing operating costs to half of what they were in 1994. The government says it spent some 10 billion forints ($60 million) to get MHB into saleable condition.

"Actually the whole bank is under restructuring and this takes a long time," Jarai told Reuters. "That's what we must tell investors -- that we just started and according to my opinion it will take three or four years."

Jarai has ambitious plans to plunge MHB into electronic banking through its Nepbank (People's Bank) subsidiary, which should begin operations next year. He wants to install automatic teller machines throughout Hungary -- in existing MHB offices, on railway platforms and in shops.
Hungary, he says, is "underbanked" with only 400,000 credit or debit cards in use compared to some five million in Portugal, which has the same population of around 10 million.
But expanding retail banking and entering the insurance market -- another goal -- will take cash.

"The capital position of the bank is really weak," Jarai said. "We achieved the eight percent capital (reserve) requirement...but honestly the capital is enough for these existing activities but not for financing further development.
"That's why we are looking for a partner bank who would increase the capital."
Abel, bluntly, says MHB may not survive without a buyer.

"It is very weak in terms of capital, products and everything because they cut so much," he said. "This is a cleaner bank (than K&H) and that's why it's more attractive to a strategic partner but if no transaction comes soon it is a failed bank."
Abel said K&H actually began clearing its books earlier than MHB, but took a more cautious approach with the result that the "cleaning is still in progress".
"K&H has no immediate problem. They can struggle for quite a long time and slowly improve but because of this messy situation the strategic investor is not that enthusiastic to step in," he said.
K&H, Hungary's third largest commercial bank, said in May this year it expected 1996 profits to stay around last year's levels, at about 1.8 billion to two billion forints.
The bank said it hoped to begin an international privatisation road show in September.
